theme: Kings, priests, prophets, the offices typology
readingInstruction: Read Deuteronomy 17:1-18:22. Having paused to see where the offices lead, return now to the text itself. This reading describes how judges, kings, priests, and prophets are to function in Israel. Look especially at the instructions for the king.
settingTheScene: Moses sets out how Israel’s offices are to work. Chapter 17 covers the administration of justice and, remarkably, a law for kings, though Israel has no king yet. Chapter 18 covers the Levitical priests and the prophets. Together they describe how God intended to govern his people under his law, with every office limited by the word of God.
observation: A person accused of idolatry is to be convicted on “the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses” (17:2-7).
Hard cases are to be taken to the Levitical priests and the judge at the place the LORD chooses (17:8-13).
“When you come to the land… and you say, I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me, you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose” (17:14-15).
The king “must not acquire many horses for himself… neither shall he acquire many wives for himself… nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold” (17:16-17).
He is to write for himself a copy of the law and “read in it all the days of his life” (17:18-19).
This is so that “his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers” (17:20).
The Levites have no inheritance among their brothers: “The LORD is his inheritance” (18:1-8).
Israel is forbidden to practice divination, sorcery, or spiritism. The LORD will raise up a prophet like Moses, and false prophets are to be tested by whether their words come to pass (18:9-22).
interpretation:
The law of the king is one of the most remarkable passages in the Old Testament. Written centuries before Israel’s first king, it limits his power in advance. The king is to be chosen by God, he is to be one of the people, he must not accumulate horses, wives, or wealth, and he must read the law every day. The only checks on ancient kings were usually other kings. Here the check is the word of God.

Look at the three prohibitions. Horses represent military power, and especially a return to Egypt, the source of horses. Wives represent political alliances, and also divided loyalties. Silver and gold represent wealth and the temptation to trust in it. Each is a way of relying on something other than God. Solomon, the wisest of kings, violated all three, and his story shows what happens when the instructions are ignored.

The king’s key duty is positive: he must write out a copy of the law with his own hand, keep it with him, and read it all his life. The result is humility, so that “his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers.” A king who knows the law knows that he is under it. The best leaders are those who submit to a higher authority.

The prophet is the last office. Moses promises that God will raise up a prophet like him. In the immediate sense, this is a promise of a line of prophets who will speak for God. But the singular, “a prophet like me,” and the later note in Deuteronomy 34:10 that no prophet had yet risen like Moses, led Israel to look for one greater prophet. The test of a true prophet is simple: his words must be God’s words, and they must prove true.

The Levites’ situation is described again: no inheritance, because the LORD is their inheritance. Those who serve at God’s altar share in the offerings. They live by faith.
connection: Jesus is the king who does not seek his own glory, who humbled himself and became obedient to death (Philippians 2:6-8). He is the king who knew the law perfectly and answered temptation with the words of Deuteronomy. He is the prophet like Moses, and Peter says so in Acts 3:22. He is also the one who calls false prophets to account (Matthew 7:15-20), and who is himself the standard by which they are measured (1 John 4:1-3).
application:
If you have any role of authority, read the law of the king as a mirror. Where are you tempted toward power, status, or wealth?

Commit to a daily reading of Scripture, as the king was to do.

Test what you hear from teachers against the word of God.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to keep you from the pride of power.
Ask him to make you a daily reader of his word.
Thank Jesus, the true king and prophet who humbled himself for you.
